text:
YOU CANNOT CURE DIARRHOEA BY STITCHING THE ANUS: Vendors are not the disease. Poverty is.

ZimRights Statement on the ultimatum by the Minister Hon Daniel Garwe September 2026

The Zimbabwe Human Rights Association (ZimRights) has noted with deep concern the directive issued on 2 September 2026 by the Minister of Local Government and Public Works, Hon. Daniel Garwe, giving vendors operating outside designated sites until 9 September 2026 to vacate the streets ahead of a nationwide "clean-up" operation beginning in Harare.

There is an old wisdom in our communities, “you cannot cure diarrhoea by stitching the anus!” The sickness is not in the street. It is in an economy that has closed its doors to its own children. Sweeping vendors off the pavement will not create a single job, will not lower the price of a single loaf of bread, and will not return a single family to dignity. It will only push the symptom out of sight while the disease deepens.

ZimRights does not dispute that our cities need order. Sanitation, safe pavements and properly serviced marketplaces are themselves rights questioned, and vendors have been asking for them for years. But order imposed by a seven-day ultimatum and municipal police, in the absence of any credible alternative, is not order. It is displacement, and it punishes the poor for the failure of the economy to accommodate them.

Before they are vendors, they are mothers, fathers, sons and daughters. They are graduates whose degrees are folded in drawers, retrenched workers, widows, young people who came of age in a country that had no vacancy for their ambition. Nobody dreams of a life spent under the sun bargaining over tomatoes and airtime. Vending is not a choice; it is the last item on a long list of things that did not work out. Strip away the label "illegal vendor" and what remains is a citizen chasing a livelihood in a country with too little to offer and inequalities too flagrant to ignore.

This demand is not new, and it is not ours alone. In 2023, after nationwide consultations, ZimRights compiled The People's Human Rights Manifesto — ten Asks that citizens placed before every aspiring Councillor, Member of Parliament and President, and which candidates signed by way of a Commitment Card. Ask 6 obliged leaders to protect and promote livelihoods, and specifically to fight for informal-sector workers to have safe spaces to ply their trade and support to grow their businesses, and to remove obstacles that prevent Zimbabweans from engaging in lawful economic activity. Ask 4 demanded that no citizen sleeps on an empty stomach. Ask 5 reminded leaders that children belong in the classroom, not vending in the streets. Ask 10 reminded them that the authority to govern comes from the people. An operation that clears the poor from the pavement without work to replace it breaks that pact.

Zimbabwe's Constitution binds the State to secure work and decent livelihoods (Section 24), to protect human dignity (Section 51), and to act lawfully, fairly and reasonably in administrative conduct (Section 68). The International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights and the African Charter require that any measure affecting people's means of subsistence be preceded by genuine consultation, adequate notice and viable alternatives. A deadline is not consultation. An eviction is not a livelihoods policy.

ZimRights therefore calls on the Government of Zimbabwe to:
1.Suspend the 9 September deadline and open structured dialogue with vendor associations, local authorities and civil society.
2.Sequence the policy correctly, provide serviced, accessible and affordable marketplaces before, not after, removals.
3.Guarantee that no enforcement involves violence, arbitrary arrest, or the destruction and confiscation of goods, which for many families is their entire capital.
4.Deliver on Ask 6 of the People’s Human Rights Manifesto, that is, safe spaces for informal traders, support to grow their businesses, and the removal of barriers to lawful economic activity.
5.Address the root causes - job creation, industrial revival, and an honest reckoning with the corruption and misgovernance that hollowed out the formal economy.

The measure of a nation is not how clean its streets look on the day of an operation. It is whether its people can eat, and hope, and dream. Let us treat the sickness, not stitch the symptom.

Issued by
Zimbabwe Human Rights Association (ZimRights) Information Department

text:
So SportyBet has been trending, and for the weirdest reason…

Many are saying their winnings were denied, some said the odds changed mid-game after they had staked, while others said money was deducted from their wallets.

But here is the full amebo…

Betting is already a huge part of Nigerian pop culture. The idea of staking small money and getting back huge rewards is just too much of a temptation in Nigeria, especially for mostly unemployed youths.

And social media made it even more popular, with the rise of betting punters and several testimonies from people who had betted with little money and somehow had a grass-to-grace story.

This is where SportyBet comes in…

The company had become a de facto favourite for online sports betting, made popular by punters and its social effect, where users can share their Sporty code and other people can play it.

Now you see why it is kinda weird for netizens to be calling for a boycott.

Because for Nigerian youths, boycotting something like SportyBet, which promises a relatively “low-risk” chance to leave the trenches… you'd know that water don pass garri.

It started late last month, when a popular Twitter punter, @JustBelieveTips, posted that SportyBet had forced a cashout of ₦3,565.99 on a slip he described as having a ₦200 million potential payout.

His followers started reporting similar glitches too, and they were livid, calling out SportyBet.

Then in early September, another X user, @lanrelndn, alleged that he won ₦3.9 million, but SportyBet claimed he had cashed out when he hadn't, which he described as an obvious glitch in their system.

To make matters worse, he said SportyBet’s customer care treated the matter trivially.

On top of almost ₦4 million?

In this economy?

Omoh.

That fuelled another round of gbas gbos.

People started showing how SportyBet glitches had allegedly made them lose money they had won from bets, and demanded that they be compensated.

But these glitches didn't just start.

Earlier this year, on the final UCL league-phase day, users said open bets and cashouts stopped working for about 90 minutes after kick-off and only came back after full-time.

SportyBet later said it was a technical fault, apologised, and some users in Nigeria and Ghana reported receiving stake refunds and free bets.

And this wasn't the first major SportyBet controversy either.

Back in 2024, over 100 customers, through Pro-lex Solicitors, said SportyBet had blocked their accounts and was sitting on winnings totalling around ₦950 million.

SportyBet’s defence then was that the accounts were linked to bots and illegal automated betting.

The users were not having it.

In no time, petitions were sent to the EFCC, police fraud units, FCCPC, NLRC and NDPC.

SportyBet themselves were not playing. They sued some customers, asking them to stop talking about the company on social media, and demanded ₦50 million in damages.

Court dismissed SportyBet’s suit… and till today, it's not clear how the matter was resolved or if the customers were compensated.

So you see…

Nigerians have had a bitter-sweet relationship with SportyBet.

Some say it changed their lives. Others are moving to other platforms and calling SportyBet a fraud. And some people are total advocates against betting altogether.

One thing is for sure: whether SportyBet is a victim of cancel culture or not, as long as unemployment is high and the economy is tough, Nigerians will bet.

Cast your bets upon many waters, for you shall win after many days.

text:
🚨 Exposing a brand in India? 

Before you post, you need to know if they can actually get your video taken down for speaking your truth."

[Do Not Skip This Part]👇
Note: This tweet is only for general understanding of how this happens. A recent tracking down of a video involving the brand has occurred. Here is a thread to understand how it happens. Please refrain from mentioning the brand name or creator name in comments or replies to this tweet. 
 
In India, there is no simple rule allowing a brand to remove a video simply because it criticizes the brand. 

The usual route is a mix of:

IT Act + IT Rules + platform policy + civil court injunction/defamation/commercial disparagement suit.

1) What is the core legal structure?

Platforms like YouTube, X, Instagram, etc. are treated as intermediaries. They get “safe harbor” protection for user-generated content, but they may lose that protection if they ignore valid legal directions.

Under India’s intermediary framework, a platform gets legally strong “actual knowledge” mainly through:

A court order, or
A government/authorized agency direction/intimation

A private brand complaint alone usually does not automatically force a platform to remove a video. 

The Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India - clarified that platforms should not be forced to decide legality merely based on private complaints; the stronger trigger is a court order or government direction.

2) How does a brand complaint become a court order?

The structure usually works like this:

Step 1: The brand's legal team collects evidence

The company gathers the video URL, transcript, screenshots, claims made in the video, alleged false statements, impact on reputation, possible business loss, and proof of harm.

Step 2: The brand's legal team may send a legal notice

This is often the first pressure step. The brand may demand a takedown, an apology, a correction, damages, or the removal of specific claims.

Step 3: The brand files a civil/commercial suit.

If the creator does not comply, the brand can file a case for defamation, commercial disparagement, trademark issues, unfair trade practice, or reputational/business harm.

Step 4: The brand asks for urgent interim relief

The brand may request an interim injunction, sometimes ex parte, meaning the court can issue a temporary order without first hearing the creator if it believes urgent harm may occur.

Step 5: The court checks the matter prima facie

At this stage, the court is not finally deciding who is right. It checks whether there is an arguable case that the content may be false, misleading, malicious, defamatory, or commercially disparaging.

Step 6: The court may pass an injunction

The order can direct the creator to remove the video, stop sharing it, stop repeating certain claims, or restrain publication of similar allegedly disparaging content.

Step 7: The court order is sent to the platform
Once YouTube/X/Instagram receives the order, the platform may remove or disable access to the video to comply and protect its intermediary safe harbor.

3) Does the brand need to contact the platform grievance officer?

They can, but for defamation or brand-disparagement disputes, the platform may not want to act purely on the brand’s private complaint unless the violation is very clear under platform policy.

The more powerful route is:

Brand → Court → Court order → Platform compliance

The grievance officer becomes important when the platform receives a complaint, legal notice, or court/government order. But the grievance officer is not usually the final judge of whether a review is defamatory or fair criticism.

4) Can a video be removed just because it criticizes a company?

No. Criticism alone should not be enough.

A creator can usually criticize a product, company, service, pricing, quality, privacy policy, design, marketing claims, or consumer experience.

But risk increases when the video makes strong factual claims, such as:

“this phone is fake”
“this company is cheating customers”
“this is just a rebranded phone”
“do not buy this because the company is lying”
“this brand is a scam”

These claims need proof. If the creator presents them as facts and the company says they are false, misleading, malicious, or damaging to business, the company may go to court.

5) What does the court usually look at?

For a temporary injunction, the court may consider:

Prima facie case: Is there an arguable case that the content is false, misleading, defamatory, or commercially disparaging?

Balance of convenience: Who will suffer more harm if the order is or is not granted?

Irreparable harm: Can the damage to reputation or business be fixed later with money, or is immediate restraint needed?

Proof and testing: Did the creator rely on reliable documents, technical tests, expert analysis, official sources, or only assumptions?

Language used: Was the tone fair and analytical, or aggressive and conclusive without enough proof?

6) What can the creator do after an ex parte order?

The creator can challenge the order in the same court. 

They can ask the court to vacate or modify the injunction and argue that:
the video was fair comment,
the claims were based on evidence,
the company suppressed facts,
the order was passed without hearing the creator,
the takedown is too broad,
or public interest requires the video to remain available.

7) Practical creator lesson

A review video is safer when it clearly separates:

Opinion: “In my view, this looks like poor value.”

Fact: “The model number matches X device.”

Evidence: screenshots, teardown, software logs, official filings, import data, product pages, privacy policy, benchmark/test method.

Limitations: “Based on my testing,” “I could not independently verify X,” “the brand has been contacted for comment.”

The danger zone is when the creator makes a strong factual allegation without showing a reliable testing method or source.

Important point:
Fair criticism is not illegal. But factual claims like “fake phone”, “rebranded phone”, “scam”, “company is cheating” need strong proof.

Disclaimer: I have shared only how the law is applied in such cases; this tweet does not reflect my opinion or view on any similar incident. 

Bookmark this for the future; this will be useful for a lot of creators out there.

text:
[15] Essential Social Media Stories for Professionals
https://t.co/g2mjT3MUUt

According to Press Monitor's media intelligence tracking of Indian publications, this press review covers 15 essential stories — news on social media regulation, platform accountability, and digital discourse. From regulatory actions to corporate disputes, these stories define the evolving relationship between social platforms and Indian society.

1. Mann Wife Defamation Restraint
A front-page report in Times of India says a district court in Chandigarh Wednesday restrained SAD leader Bikram Singh Majithia, Congress MLA Sukhpal Singh Khaira and retired Punjab and Haryana High Court judge Justice Ranjit Singh from posting unverified or allegedly defamatory material against Punjab Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann's wife Dr Gurpreet Kaur on social media or any other medium until further orders. The court passed the interim order while hearing a defamation petition filed by Kaur against the three respondents on September 8, relating to allegations that she had demanded Rs 5 crore to help suppress a rape case. The next hearing is scheduled for September 30.
Why it matters: The Chandigarh court's interim order sets a significant precedent for online speech boundaries involving public figures in Indian politics. Key detail: Three respondents — SAD leader Bikram Singh Majithia, Congress MLA Sukhpal Singh Khaira, and retired judge Justice Ranjit Singh — are barred until further orders, with the next hearing on September 30. Source: Times of India and Tribune. Next step: Political offices across India will likely issue social media compliance guidelines. Closing: Will this ruling reshape how politicians and their supporters engage on digital platforms?

2. Meta Executives Appear Before NCPCR
A front-page report in Financial Express says senior executives of Meta appeared before the National Child Rights Protection Council on Wednesday in connection with the inquiry into alleged advertisements featuring child sexual exploitation and abuse material on the platform.
Why it matters: This appearance signals tightening regulatory scrutiny of global social media platforms operating in India, reinforcing the need for robust media monitoring. Key detail: Senior Meta executives discussed alleged child sexual exploitation advertisements on the platform with the National Commission for Protection of Child Rights. Source: Financial Express and The Pioneer. Next step: Expect Meta to announce enhanced content moderation policies for the Indian market. Closing: How will global platforms balance free expression with child protection obligations?

3. Meta Faces New Mexico Privacy Lawsuit
A front-page report in The Pioneer says New Mexico will begin opening statements on Wednesday in Santa Fe state court against Meta over privacy violations tied to user data harvested during the twenty sixteen election for targeted advertising. State Attorney General Raul Torrez highlighted that the social media giant's actions exposed a consistent pattern of misrepresenting how user information was collected. While forty eight other United States states recently reached a landmark settlement with the company, New Mexico pursued independent legal action alongside Florida, which also declined to join the broader agreement.
Why it matters: New Mexico's independent legal action against Meta over 2016 election data harvesting shows that state-level privacy enforcement is gaining momentum globally. Key detail: While 48 US states reached a landmark settlement, New Mexico and Florida pursued separate legal action, highlighting persistent concerns about user data misuse. Source: The Pioneer. Next step: Monitor for similar state-level actions that could influence Indian data protection debates. Closing: Can state-level litigation force meaningful change in how social platforms handle user data?

4. Subhash Chandra Sues Social Media Platforms
A front-page report in Business Line says Subhash Chandra, founder of Zee Entertainment Enterprises, has sent letters threatening to sue Meta, YouTube, X, and LinkedIn India for defamation over content about his personal insolvency case. He gave the platforms a week to correct information about a repayment plan approved by the National Company Law Tribunal. Chandra claims his borrowing was nil and he was only a personal guarantor.
Why it matters: Zee Entertainment founder Subhash Chandra's defamation threat against Meta, YouTube, X, and LinkedIn India underscores the growing use of legal action against social platforms in India. Key detail: Chandra claims his borrowing was nil and he was only a personal guarantor, disputing reports about his insolvency case. Source: Business Line. Next step: Watch for platform responses and potential legal counterarguments. Closing: Will defamation claims become a new tool for shaping online discourse?

5. Delhi Airport Fake Waterlogging Video FIR
A front-page report in Hindustan Times says police registered an FIR against 63 social media handles for circulating a misleading video claiming waterlogging at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport was actually old footage from Dubai. The case, filed on September 6, invoked sections of the BNS and IT Act accusing the operators of spreading misinformation to defame a critical public utility. Authorities clarified that while heavy rainfall caused temporary water accumulation at Terminal 3's arrival forecourt, operations were never affected and the situation was resolved within 20 minutes.
Why it matters: Police action against 63 social media handles demonstrates authorities' increasing willingness to pursue misinformation targeting critical public infrastructure. Key detail: An old Dubai airport waterlogging video was falsely claimed as Delhi airport footage; operations were never affected and resolved within 20 minutes. Source: Hindustan Times and The Pioneer. Next step: Expect more FIRs under the IT Act as viral misinformation continues to spread. Closing: How can social media users verify content before sharing it with their networks?

6. Singapore Questions Five Over Racist Posts
A front-page report in The Pioneer says that Singapore police have questioned five individuals aged between twenty nine and sixty six regarding racist and xenophobic online comments about the Nepal floods and Singapore Airlines investment in Air India. Home Affairs Minister K Shanmugam condemned the remarks, noting they incite hostility despite thousands affected by the disaster. Authorities are actively investigating the cases and have urged social media platforms to remove content violating community guidelines.
Why it matters: Singapore's enforcement against racist online comments about Nepal floods and Air India investment shows growing global accountability for social media speech. Key detail: Home Affairs Minister K Shanmugam condemned remarks inciting hostility, and authorities urged platforms to remove violating content. Source: The Pioneer. Next step: Watch for cross-border cooperation on social media regulation. Closing: Should racist online speech face international consequences?

7. Ajit Mohan Steps Down as Snapchat CBO
A front-page report in Business Standard says Snapchat’s chief business officer Ajit Mohan has decided to step down after four years, citing personal reasons to return to India. Ronan Harris will replace him as CBO at Snap, and Mohan will remain at the company until the end of the calendar year.
Why it matters: Leadership changes at major social platforms directly impact advertising strategies and monetization in key markets like India. Key detail: Ajit Mohan steps down after four years citing personal reasons to return to India; Ronan Harris will replace him as CBO. Source: Business Standard. Next step: Monitor Snap's India advertising strategy under new leadership. Closing: What does this mean for Snapchat's growth in the Indian market?

8. Saadia Azim's Book on Disinformation
A front-page report in Business Standard says Saadia Azim's book Forwarded as Received examines the spread of misinformation and disinformation in contemporary India. The book highlights how fake news has led to real-world violence, including the lynching of Mohammad Akhlaq in Uttar Pradesh in 2015. Azim argues that rebuilding trust and digital literacy, rather than censorship, is the way forward.
Why it matters: Saadia Azim's Forwarded as Received offers a compelling framework for combating disinformation through digital literacy rather than censorship — a critical conversation for media intelligence. Key detail: The book highlights how fake news led to real-world violence, including the lynching of Mohammad Akhlaq in 2015, and proposes prebunking mechanisms. Source: Business Standard. Next step: Expect broader conversations about platform accountability for disinformation. Closing: Can digital literacy alone solve the misinformation crisis?

9. DIAL Files FIR Against 63 Social Media Handles
A front-page report in The Pioneer says Delhi airport operator DIAL filed a First Information Report against 63 social media handles for circulating misleading content about flooding at Terminal 3 last week. DIAL stated that while heavy rainfall caused temporary water accumulation on September 4, 2026, airport operations were not affected and the situation was resolved within 20 minutes. An old video of waterlogging at Dubai airport was among the posts falsely claimed to show the Delhi airport.
Why it matters: Delhi airport operator DIAL's direct legal action against misinformation shows public infrastructure entities are taking social media accountability seriously. Key detail: An old Dubai airport video was among posts falsely claiming Delhi airport flooding; the situation was resolved within 20 minutes. Source: The Pioneer. This comes after a trial court denied him relief earlier this month. Separately, a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana noted that no grave or heinous crimes were alleged in a different set of cases, which included burning of effigies and dharnas.
Why it matters: Social media influencer Ajeet Bharti's bail application raises fundamental questions about free expression boundaries for digital creators in India. Key detail: The Delhi High Court is considering his SC/ST Act case after a trial court denied relief earlier this month. Source: Free Press Journal. Separately, the top court allowed the Himachal Pradesh government to withdraw prosecution against some sitting or former MLAs in several criminal cases registered during the COVID-19 pandemic. The article emphasizes the role of unpaid mental-health carers and urges communities to respond with compassion rather than shame to help people seek support before reaching a crisis point.
Why it matters: Social media platforms face growing responsibility for mental health content, especially when distressing videos of suicides go viral and cause further trauma. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s announcement of a tax holiday from FY 2026-27 to FY 2067-2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services using Indian data centres has been interpreted as a reassurance to hyperscalers worried about permanent establishment risk. On the surface, that reading is correct. However, a deeper look reveals that the development masks a more interesting economic dynamic. 

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman’s announcement of a tax holiday from FY 2026-27 to FY 2067-2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services using Indian data centres has been interpreted as a reassurance to hyperscalers worried about permanent establishment risk. On the surface, that reading is correct.

However, a deeper look reveals that the development masks a more interesting economic dynamic. This measure will reshape the sharing of additional profits across the entire cloud value chain in India, benefiting not just the foreign tech giants, but also domestic data centre operators, Indian resellers, and—in ways often overlooked—Indian and global customers of cloud services.

The Budget 2026 exemption, on the face of it, applies to any foreign company earning “by procuring data centre services from a specified data centre” in India, with an exemption valid till March 2047. On first read, it seems to be a comfort measure for multinational companies such as AWS (Amazon), Microsoft, Google and Meta. Following several Supreme Court of India rulings, these companies feared that locating substantial infrastructure in India would trigger permanent establishment status, thus exposing them to Indian taxation on their global cloud revenues.

But here is the underlying operative constraint—the data centre must be owned and operated by an Indian company, notified under an approved scheme by the IT ministry. And, any sales to Indian customers must flow through an Indian reseller entity, typically the Indian subsidiary of the cloud firm or a domestic partner, which remains fully taxable in India with a 15 per cent safe harbour margin on costs.

What the Budget has done, in other words, is to trade away a potential tax claim on foreign cloud income in exchange for irreversible hard investment on Indian soil. The foreign company pays zero tax on a particular income stream; India ensures that data centre ownership, reseller involvement and domestic value-addition remain tethered to domestic companies, with massive, high-cost infrastructure on Indian soil.

Who benefits, and why the sequencing matters 

The primary beneficiary, as intended, is the foreign hyperscaler. AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud and Meta have collectively announced around $67.5 billion of data centre and AI-related investments in India over the next five years. The tax holiday reduces their after-tax cost of using Indian capacity relative to hosting the same workloads in Singapore, the UAE or Europe, making India far more competitive for global cloud workloads. 

But the chain reaction begins here. The foreign cloud’s improved after-tax return immediately raises its willingness-to-pay for Indian data centre capacity. In a market where power, cooling and suitable land are scarce—as India races to build gigawatt-scale compute infrastructure—that willingness-to-pay gets reflected in higher lease rates and better contract terms negotiated with Indian data centre operators.

Those operators are India’s emerging infrastructure barons—AdaniConneX (targeting 1 GW capacity), Reliance Jio, Tata group platforms, Airtel’s Nxtra (commanding 15 per cent market share), Yotta Infrastructure, CtrlS, Sify and others. They are racing to create AI-ready facilities across Mumbai, Chennai, Hyderabad, Visakhapatnam, Noida and Pune. The tax holiday does not directly benefit them—they continue to pay corporate tax as usual—but it indirectly bolsters their negotiating position and pricing power by making foreign customers more willing to pay premium rates for access to “specified” notified facilities.

In global data centre markets, lease rates have risen sharply over 2023–2025 because AI and cloud demand have outstripped available power and cooling and, of course, high-performance GPUs. India’s operators, now assured that their primary foreign customers enjoy long-duration tax certainty, can capture a meaningful share of the additional profits generated by this bold income tax holiday through higher capacity pricing, coming on top of India’s ambitious Superconductor Mission, which envisages up to 50 per cent open-ended capital subsidy for domestic manufacturing of GPUs.

The reseller ecosystem and cloud customers 

The Budget structure mandates that Indian reseller entities—AWS India, Microsoft India, Google Cloud India, cloud arms of IT majors like TCS, Infosys and Wipro, and telecom-embedded providers—be part of the sales chain when claiming the exemption for Indian customer sales. The 15 per cent safe harbour rules, also a part of this Budget, on related-party data centre service costs signal policy comfort with a layered value chain and protect reseller margins.

Indian and global consumers of cloud services—startups, SMEs, enterprises and SaaS firms—stand to benefit from the competitive intensity that this tax holiday catalyses. As competition among hyperscalers deepens and capacity expands, some of the additional profits will pass through as more competitive cloud pricing, lowering barriers to digital adoption and improving margins for businesses reliant on India-hosted infrastructure. 

The political economy of how this is presented matters. Announcing a “tax holiday for foreign cloud providers till 2047 reads as a necessary course correction; announcing what the opposition could frame as “20-year tax holiday for data centre conglomerates like Adani, Reliance and Tata” would draw harsher scrutiny. By routing the direct benefit through the foreign entity while hard-wiring Indian ownership, the government has elegantly packaged a very substantial infrastructure incentive inside a narrative of global openness.

This is a political skill. But it is worth being explicit: the Budget’s measure is as much about anchoring hard assets and Indian ownership as it is about welcoming foreign clouds.

Why long-term certainty was necessary

There is, however, a compelling policy case—and indeed, this bold and substantial income tax holiday is quite justified. Data centres are the physical backbone of cloud computing and AI. As workloads grow heavier, hosting capacity within national borders becomes a question of digital sovereignty. India has already moved in that direction through data localisation norms and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act.

The Budget’s tax holiday is a fiscal complement to that regulatory thrust: it says to foreign clouds, “Bring compute and workloads to India; we will not use the tax system to ambush you”—but Indian ownership and domestic intermediaries remain non-negotiable.

Viewed this way, the measure is not a disguised giveaway but a conscious, well-crafted and necessary concession: India forgoes contested tax claims in exchange for encouraging irreversible hard investment, in the order of billions of dollars, on Indian soil. That is reasonable for a country betting on becoming a global cloud hub and a centre of AI capability. 

The winners are multiple: foreign hyperscalers gain tax certainty; Indian data centre operators gain pricing power and volume; Indian resellers gain regulated margins and market growth; cloud customers gain access to cheaper, more competitive services anchored in India. It is a policy that aligns incentives across the entire value chain while preserving domestic ownership and taxable profit pools.

The packaging is clever. The economics are sound.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

Here's #ThePrintOpinion by KBS Sidhu @kbssidhu1961 

The Union government’s draft Seeds Bill 2025, now open for public comments until 11 December, arrives not a day too soon. From counterfeit packets in village markets to procurement disputes at mandis, the chain between breeder and farmer has too many weak links.

For Punjab, where seed quality, FCI norms, and groundwater stress intersect, if not collide, every season, this Bill is more than a compliance document. It is a chance to rebuild trust in the most basic input of agriculture.

How is it better than the old law?

Three design shifts from the Seeds Act of 1966 deserve unambiguous support.

First, universal registration of varieties. The 1966 Act essentially regulated only ‘notified’ kinds, leaving a grey market of truthfully labelled seeds outside meaningful oversight. The draft moves toward mandatory registration for all new varieties and a pathway for deemed registration of existing ones. If implemented with predictable timelines and transparent criteria, this closes the back door through which poor-quality seed has circulated for decades.

Second, traceability and digital oversight. The draft emphasises traceability— already feasible through platforms that assign a scannable identity to each lot from breeder to dealer. That lets a farmer verify authenticity at the counter and allows regulators to trace a bad lot swiftly up the chain. Traceability should not be a slogan; it must become a farmer’s everyday tool. Make it mandatory at scale, standardise the QR/barcode, and integrate it with e-invoices so that one scan reveals who produced, processed, stored, and sold the seed, and when.

Third, smarter penalties with measured decriminalisation. Minor technical lapses should not land honest actors in criminal court; serious fraud should. The draft’s graded penalties, with steep fines and custodial terms for spurious and unregistered seed, are a clear improvement over the token fines of the 1966 law. The promise is a system that is both business-friendly and farmer‑protective—if enforcement stays sharp.

Two related moves are consequential for Punjab. One is the shift from a state-by-state dealer licensing culture to centralised accreditation/recognition. That may cut duplication for multi-state firms, but it also risks hollowing out the “last mile” unless states retain day-to-day inspection teeth. The other is price oversight “in emergent situations”. That clause matters in the sowing window, when speculation can shut smallholders out of quality seed.

Federal design at the last mile

The August ruling of the Punjab and Haryana High Court, which held that states cannot ban centrally notified hybrid paddy, was a reminder that seed regulation sits across the Centre-state seam. Punjab has since hardened deterrence at its end, making the sale of spurious seeds a non-bailable, cognisable offence, reflecting accumulated anger in the countryside at fly-by-night operators. Industry protests aside, the message from Chandigarh is clear: the deterrent must be felt in the marketplace.

The draft national law should recognise this reality instead of flattening it. Keep national registration and central accreditation if you must—but codify concurrent enforcement powers for states: surprise sampling, seizure, prosecution, and the ability to prescribe local storage and display conditions. Delhi can set standards; inspectors in Moga and Muktsar will enforce them.

Farmers’ vantage point: performance and procurement

From a farmer’s field, regulation is judged by three blunt questions: Did the seed perform? If not, who pays? And will the crop be procured on fair terms?

The draft is strong at the pre-market gate (registration and traceability) and on deterrence. It is notably weaker on compensation when registered seed underperforms despite adoption of the recommended package of practices. Punjab’s last two seasons underlined why this gap matters: disruptive weather, discolouration and moisture contests at mandis, and a milling reluctance toward some hybrids have turned quality disputes into income shocks.

The fix is straightforward. Create a time-bound, no-fault compensation window for clear seed failures, financed by a blend of mandatory manufacturer insurance, a small cess on registrations, and state top-ups in disaster years. Publish the yield-loss formula up front; do not force a small farmer to litigate against a corporate legal team. At the same time, institutionalise pre-season coordination among the Agriculture Ministry, FCI/DFPD, and states on uniform procurement specifications, with a hybrid-specific annexure and pre-declared relaxations for flood years. Let seed standards and procurement norms talk to each other before the first bag is sold.

Let FPOs co-brand seed

Earlier seed‑bill drafts recognised a farmer’s right to save, use, exchange and sell farm‑saved seed, with one caveat: it cannot be sold under a brand name.

The intent was to block quasi‑commercial masquerading without quality assurance. But the rise of Farmer Producer Organisations (FPOs) changes the calculus. The Union government wants FPOs to aggregate, process, and market produce; it funds them and extends credit and tax support for precisely that reason. If the final Seeds Act mechanically extends a “no brand” caveat to FPO‑aggregated seed, it would hobble a flagship reform.

The harmonising path is clear: permit FPO co-branding of farm-saved seed provided three conditions are met. First, lots must pass notified minimum standards in an accredited lab. Second, full traceability, including grower IDs and storage logs that must be uploaded to the national portal. Third, liability must sit with the FPO’s board for false claims, not with individual members. That keeps out fly-by-night branding while letting farmer institutions move up the value chain.

Dealer liability, without scapegoating the honest

Punjab has thousands of small input dealers who act as the farmer’s first line of advice and supply. They cannot become the system’s whipping boy for failures they did not cause.

The law should adopt a manufacturer-first liability rule on germination and genetic purity for factory-sealed packs, while giving dealers a safe harbour if they sell sealed lots, meet prescribed storage conditions, keep traceable invoices, and hand over required samples during inspections. Penal exposure should bite dealers who tamper, knowingly misbrand, or operate outside the accredited chain. That keeps deterrence where it belongs—on those who cheat—without driving legitimate retailers out of business.

Traceability as a price stabiliser, not just a cop’s tool

If the Centre retains emergency price-control powers, anchor them in transparent triggers captured by the traceability system: inventory-to-sowing-window ratios, abnormal interstate price spreads, and unusual movement patterns. Public dashboards would discipline prices before official fiat is needed, and they would help states intervene in time. Let the QR on a packet be both a shield against fraud and a signal for markets.

Water‑wise seed choices backed by procurement

For Punjab, seed policy is also water policy. Short-duration, water-efficient paddy, as well as non-paddy kharif options, must get fast-track registration and agronomy support.

But farmers will not switch varieties or crops unless procurement policy aligns. That means assured purchase pathways for water-saving options, predictable miller acceptance for hybrids, and extension support that links seed choice to groundwater outcomes. Otherwise, the rational farmer will cling to long-duration staples that mills prefer and FCI buys on familiar specs.

It is essential to stitch seed regulation to FCI procurement policy for hybrid paddy so that what farmers sow confidently in June is not rejected quibblingly in October.

Minor tweaks before enactment: a Punjab‑first checklist

Keep central registration, but write state enforcement powers into the statute.

Clarify the liability chain: manufacturer first; dealer safe harbour for sealed, properly stored, traceable stock; strict penalties for tampering and misbranding.

Make compensation real with a time‑bound, no‑fault window and a published formula.

Hard‑wire coordination with FCI on uniform specs and a hybrid‑specific annexure, with pre‑declared relaxations in disaster years.

Use traceability to improve competition and price discovery, not merely to police.

Greenlight FPO co‑branding under standards‑plus‑traceability, with board‑level liability.

Invest in accredited seed labs and risk‑based inspections so enforcement is fast, fair and science‑led.

The draft Seeds Bill, 2025 gets the big ideas right: universal registration, traceability, and real penalties. To work for Punjab’s farmers, it must now get the federal plumbing and farmer-facing details right. If the suggestions above are incorporated, India will finally plant what Punjab has long demanded: a pro-farmer, pro-federal seed law that deters the bad actors and rewards the good.

The Bombay High Court on Friday struck down the amendments to Information Technology (IT) Rules allowing the Central government to establish Fact-Check Units. 

Comedian Kunal Kamra has filed a petition against the Centre's move to establish Fact-Check Units to identify and debunk 'fake and misleading' information about its functioning on social media platforms under the Press Information Bureau (PIB).

Many journalists, politicians, and creators in India are facing similar issues; accounts being suspended, posts removed, or visibility reduced with little transparency or meaningful recourse.

These actions often happen under two parallel mechanisms of India’s Information Technology Act, 2000.

Section 69A allows the Government to issue blocking orders on broad grounds such as national security or public order. However, these orders are usually confidential, and affected users often receive neither notice nor a copy of the blocking order, making it difficult to challenge them.

Separately, Section 79(3)(b) allows authorities to pressure platforms to remove content by threatening loss of “safe harbour” protections if platforms fail to comply with government or court directions. In practice, this creates strong incentives for platforms to over-comply.

The lack of transparency around these processes raises serious concerns for due process, free expression, and accountability.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

Delhi HC’s order in Anil Kumar Tiwari (Aniruddhacharya) v. John Doe (Ashok Kumar & Ors.), CS(COMM) 336/2026 is more than a takedown of memes and deepfakes, it signals a structural shift in how India is preparing for the AI-driven future.

Key aspects of the case:

• Plaintiff: Anil Kumar Tiwari, widely known as Aniruddhacharya Ji Maharaj ("Pookie Baba")

• Defendants: John Doe (Ashok Kumar & Ors.), covering anonymous creators along with intermediaries like Meta, Google, and X

• The Problem: Circulation of AI-generated deepfakes, doctored videos, fake endorsements, and distorted spiritual discourse violating personality rights

• Court Order: Complete restraint on creating or sharing any content replicating the plaintiff’s name, voice, image, or mannerisms without authorization

• Intermediary Directions: Meta, X, and Google directed to remove, disable access, and take down all flagged content immediately

The Court (Justice Tushar Rao Gedela, 30 March 2026) granted an ex-parte ad-interim injunction, recognizing that a person’s identity is not public property but a legally enforceable asset.

The mood of this judgment is unmistakably urgent, protective, and corrective. What was once brushed off as meme culture is now being treated as structured digital harm amplified by AI.

Key judicial observations:

• Personality Rights Recognized:

The Court affirmed that a public figure’s identity carries enforceable personality and publicity rights

• Irreparable Loss:

Unauthorized AI usage causes serious reputational damage that cannot be monetarily compensated

• "Love for Delhi" Remark:

Justice Gedela interestingly questioned why such cases consistently prefer Delhi HC jurisdiction, even when defendants are anonymous, hinting at forum concentration in tech-IP disputes

What makes this ruling significant:

• Personality = IP asset
Identity is now treated as an economic and legal right, expanding India’s IP framework

• Dynamic enforcement model 
Not a one-time order, but continuous takedown authority against evolving content

• John Doe mechanism
Adapts law to the anonymous, decentralized nature of AI misuse

• Deepfakes legally elevated
No longer trivial, now recognized as causing irreversible real-world harm

The AI Reality Check:
AI itself is neutral, but its misuse is not.

Positive side:

• Creativity at scale
• Education and accessibility
• Digital economy expansion
Negative side (highlighted here):
• Fake endorsements and scams
• Reputation manipulation
• Synthetic misinformation
• Identity theft through voice and face cloning

This case shows how AI has blurred the line between satire and synthetic deception.

Impact on India’s IP & Legal Ecosystem:

This ruling strengthens:

• Recognition of persona as intellectual property
• Platform accountability (Meta, Google, X as enforcement layers)
• Early foundations of AI governance frameworks
• Evolution toward structured digital identity protection laws

It also aligns with broader regulatory momentum around AI and intermediary responsibility.
What this means for the future:

We are entering a phase where:

• Every public personality becomes a protectable digital asset

• AI systems will require consent and compliance layers

• Courts will increasingly define boundaries of AI usage

• Deepfake regulation will become unavoidable

In simple terms:

Your face, voice, and personality are becoming your most valuable IP.

Conclusion:

This is not just about one individual.
It is about protecting human identity in an era of synthetic reality.

The message is clear:

Innovation is welcome, exploitation is not.

Every @Shopify  store fighting for the 45+ demo on Fox News/ @taboola  right now is quietly doing the same thing: pushing buyers toward 3x bundles instead of single units. Here's the mechanic — and why it's about to matter a lot more 🧵

1. The gifts only unlock at the top tier

Free ebook, free cleaning brush, free travel case — all listed as "$0.00" line items in the cart. They cost the brand almost nothing to include, but visually they make the 3x option look like it comes with a whole bonus package the 1x buyer doesn't get.

2. The most expensive tier is the pre-selected default

Notice the 3x option has the filled radio button, not the cheapest 1x. Most shoppers never touch the default — so the "decision" to spend 2x more was actually made for them before they scrolled to the checkout button.

3. Escalating savings % reframes spending more as saving more

29% → 44% → 53% off as quantity goes up. The math itself argues for the bigger order. By the time a buyer reaches the 3x tier, walking away feels like leaving money on the table instead of spending more of it.

4. Urgency closes the deal before comparison shopping happens

"Items in your cart are in high demand," a live countdown reserving the order — this isn't decoration, it's designed to convert the hesitation window before a 45+ buyer opens a new tab to price-check.

5. Why this determines who wins the ad auction, not just the sale

Native placements like Fox News Taboola are won by CPC/CPM bids — and what you can afford to bid is a direct function of AOV. A store converting at $32/unit (3x bundle) has more margin to spend per click than a store stuck at $69/unit single sales. AOV isn't just revenue — it's auction firepower.

6. Why this gets more important as BFCM approaches

Every one of your competitors is about to flood the same native placements with holiday budget. CPCs on Fox News/Taboola climb hard in the BFCM run-up as demand spikes. The stores still profitable at $8-12 CPCs in November will be the ones who already engineered 3x-bundle-as-default checkouts — not the ones scrambling to test bundling for the first time during the highest-competition week of the year. Build the offer now. Don't build it in the middle of BFCM.

text:
India clearing administrative satcom spectrum at 5% AGR (4% in notified remote/border pockets) is being framed as an open runway for Starlink.

​The regulatory fine print and unit economics tell a very different story.

​What most headlines missed, and how this truly reshapes Indian telecom:
​
1. The True Cost: A 13% Total Regulatory Toll
The 5% spectrum charge isn’t the only levy. Satcom operators must still pay the standard 8% annual telecom license fee.
A total 13% AGR levy—coupled with zero terminal subsidies (the DoT rejected TRAI’s proposal to subsidize dishes via the Digital Bharat Nidhi fund)—rules out aggressive retail price dumping.
​
2. The Rejection of the Urban Disincentive
TRAI recommended a ₹500/year surcharge per urban subscriber to force operators deep into the hinterland.
The DoT scrapped it. Why? Policing dynamic satellite spot beams across fluid administrative boundaries is technically unworkable.
This greenlights high-paying, remote enterprise pockets (mining belts, maritime vessels, defense corridors, infrastructure builds, luxury eco-resorts) to cross-subsidize expensive user terminals.
​
3. Does This Threaten Jio & Airtel's Retail Broadband? No.
​ARPU Realities: Indian fibre/5G FWA already sits at ₹500–₹1,000/month. Starlink-class terminals are ₹25,000–₹40,000. That is not a home-broadband fight in tier-1 to tier-3 towns.
​Physics & Capacity: LEO is a coverage and backhaul layer. It does not replace mass retail broadband over a dense metro.

​4. The Real Competitive Playbook
​▪️$BHARTIARTL - Built an early enterprise moat. Backed by Eutelsat OneWeb, Airtel already has licensed Indian ground stations and B2B corporate contracts ready to flip the switch.
​▪️Reliance Jio: Jio Space (partnered with SES via MEO/GEO) isn't chasing rooftop dishes; they will use satcom to backhaul remote 4G/5G cell towers where laying terrestrial fiber is economically unviable.

​Domestic Satellite Ecosystem Plays:
​▪️$NELCO (Tata Group) & Hughes India: Strong legacy enterprise and maritime satcom providers that now face direct LEO competition.
​▪️$AVANTEL & $DATAPATTNS - Base station gateways, defense RF electronics, and satellite transceivers see structural domestic demand as gateway infrastructure expands.
​
Satcom in India isn't an urban consumer price war; it’s a high-margin enterprise, defense, and cellular backhaul play.

​(Educational only. Not investment advice.)

France 24. BBC. Reuters. Al Jazeera. Washington DC. Human Rights Watch.

When does a government stop calling it foreign interference and start asking, why is the entire world saying the same thing about us?

Here is what is actually happening inside India right now:

▪️ India has the world’s strictest content takedown window; just 3 hours. No major democracy, and no major authoritarian regime, moves this fast against its own citizens’ speech.

▪️ Under the new IT Rules 2026 amendment, it’s not just news outlets being targeted. Ordinary users, influencers, and anyone who simply shares a news post can now fall under the government’s content blocking framework.

▪️ The Internet Freedom Foundation has formally called this “digital authoritarianism” and a “dangerous expansion of executive power.” These are not opposition politicians, these are constitutional lawyers and digital rights experts.

▪️ Since 2014, India’s government takedown orders have surged 14 times; from 201 to 14,775. And post 2022, this data was denied under RTI on grounds of national security.

▪️ Meta alone was forced to restrict 28,000+ pieces of content in India in just the first six months of 2025; following government orders.

▪️ India currently ranks 151 out of 180 in the World Press Freedom Index. We are sitting between countries most Indians would be ashamed to be compared with.

▪️ The Supreme Court’s own Shreya Singhal judgment; a landmark free speech ruling, is being systematically bypassed by these rules.

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

Statement against arbitrary content takedown and account restrictions faced by public representatives and journalists

Earlier today, @Meta restricted the Instagram accounts (“Platform”) of @AamAadmiParty (AAP), its national convener @ArvindKejriwal, and Mohammed Zubair (@zoo_bear), co-founder of @AltNews. 

Over the past week, along with these instances, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has also recorded several instances of content takedowns faced by media organisations including @PeekTV_in, cartoonists such as @cartoonistrrs and @cartoonistvish, and @SauravDassss - @Cockroachisback's spokesperson.

According to the publicly available information, the affected posts were restricted pursuant to the “legal requests” received by the Platform. In many cases, users are provided little or no meaningful explanation about the legal or factual basis of the restriction or what steps they can take to challenge the decision. Such opaque moderation practices undermine users’ ability to understand how platform policies are enforced and make it difficult to distinguish between legitimate moderation and arbitrary or inconsistent decision-making. This is especially concerning where the affected content relates to political expression, criticism of public authorities, or peaceful protest, all of which occupy a central place in democratic discourse.

The Supreme Court of India upheld the constitutionality of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000 (“IT Act”), on the basis that the statutory framework required that blocking orders be reasoned, necessary, and proportionate, and that such reasons must be recorded in writing to enable judicial review. By contrast, in most of these cases, notices sent to social media intermediaries through the Sahyog Portal under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act and Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, leave users in the dark, with no recourse to meaningfully challenge takedowns and leave affected parties without legal redressal. The Sahyog Portal puts in place a parallel system to take down content online, without any of the safeguards present under Section 69A.

https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 has consistently advocated against these practices. We are concerned that this takedown drive is contrary to the rule of law and to India’s constitutional commitment to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution.

While private platforms are not directly bound by the Constitution in the same manner as the State, their content moderation decisions increasingly influence the digital spaces in which democratic participation takes place. This places a heightened responsibility on platforms to ensure that their moderation processes are transparent, consistently applied, and accompanied by adequate procedural safeguards, including notice, reasons for enforcement actions, and effective mechanisms for review. At the same time, any direction issued by public authorities requiring platforms to restrict lawful online speech must comply with constitutional safeguards and the legal procedures prescribed under Indian law. Informal or opaque restrictions on political speech or press freedom undermine public trust and democratic accountability.

In light of the above, https://t.co/X7ipfsWjp2 calls for the following:

- Immediate disclosure of all takedown orders issued to platforms, including specific reasons and legal justifications.

- Strict adherence to the procedural safeguards laid out under Section 69A and the 2009 Blocking Rules, under the IT Act, which were upheld by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India.

- Notices received by social media intermediaries to be sent to every user affected to ensure transparency.

- Strengthening of independent oversight and appellate mechanisms to ensure that users can effectively challenge unlawful restrictions.

- Greater transparency from platforms regarding the number, nature, source, and outcome of governmental requests/orders for content removal and account restriction.

Mercenary spyware is surveillance software deployed by government or law enforcement agencies to surveil individuals such as journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats and collect sensitive information from their devices. NIXI has changed its justification for suspending chalosansad dot in yet again. After first citing a “critical keyword”, and then relying on a 2004 policy clause that did not apply, it now invokes the Emblems Act and demands Central Government permission within seven days. On 8 September, IFF wrote back seeking a standstill and answers. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2grOxR1bMy

The timing matters. The domain was suspended on 22 July. NIXI’s new legal opinion was obtained on 29 August, more than a month later and only after we challenged its earlier reasons. The Supreme Court has repeatedly held that administrative action must stand or fall on the reasons given when the decision was made; authorities cannot ordinarily supplement an order with new reasons after it is challenged. (6/7)

NIXI has now also said that six other .in domains containing “Sansad”, along with other domains containing “Sansad”, “Parliament” or cognate expressions, will be examined. On 8 September, we asked NIXI for a 48-hour standstill on de-registration, deletion, transfer or reallocation of chalosansad dot in, confirmation of Aadhaar deletion, and disclosure of the correspondence it says raised concerns about publication. If no standstill is given, the registrant will approach the court. (7/7)

Our government suppresses dissent by criminalizing criticism

quotedTweet.text:
On September 10th, 2013, the Supreme Court struck down Section 66A of the IT Act, a vague law that was being used to arrest people for simply expressing dissent online.

11 years later, Maharashtra wants to bring it back in a new form, by amending the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for "online criminal defamation." But defamation is already covered under Section 356 of the BNS, and civil remedies already exist.

So why does the police need this new power? Recent FIRs against citizens and influencers for calling out potholes and infrastructure failures may hold the answer. We've fought this battle before. We don't need a new 66A with a new number.

text:
A 2:01-minute reel documenting villagers’ concerns over the proposed Google data centre in Visakhapatnam was blocked in India for 111 days. On 10 September 2026, it quietly came back online. (1/10)

Read More: https://t.co/TVxhdw9ZA1

The Sahyog route also raises a serious constitutional concern. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because the blocking framework contained procedural safeguards, including notice, hearing and a reasoned order. Section 79(3)(b), meanwhile, was read down to require a court order or government notification. A system that blocks first and explains nothing is difficult to reconcile with those safeguards. (9/10)

The reel is back, and we welcome that. But the questions remain unanswered, Who ordered the blocking? Why did the order name an unrelated person? Was a periodic review conducted? Why was the reel restored? IFF will continue seeking these answers from Andhra Pradesh authorities. Journalists should not need months of litigation to learn why their public-interest reporting was censored. (10/10)
